what_it_checks: The reopen ordering inside next_parent: no crossing, a crossing, and a crossing whose shift lands in a closed window.
derivation: Section 4.1 step 5 uses the crossing test from_ns < at_ts_ns <= candidate. No crossing leaves the candidate untouched. A crossing shifts the candidate, and if the shifted instant is closed the calendar's next_open_ns supplies the resolved parent. The calendar here is open through the epoch's own minute and shut for the one after it, so 70.5 s is closed and reopens at 120 s. Windows are indexed in minutes of the LOCAL week and the Unix epoch sits 5,760 minutes into that week, so clock minute 1 - the closed one - is week minute 5,761. Version 2 replaced the original ten-nanosecond arithmetic: SessionCalendar is minute-granular, so a next_open_ns of 100 ns was unreachable by any calendar and the whole vector could only be checked against a local re-implementation of the crossing rule. Each case's candidate is placed by giving next_parent a unit-intensity budget of (candidate_ns - from_ns) / 1e9 seconds, which section 4.2's time change resolves to exactly that instant; case 1 gates that placement directly, since its parent IS the unshifted candidate. Each cell below is the case's parent instant divided by the cadence step declared in params - the derivation's claim that the snapped time is also the cell, which version 2's first cut left asserting over nothing. next_from_ns carries no expected value on purpose: the child count is an RNG draw, so a pinned successor instant would be a run written down. What params does pin is the stride the identity multiplies by.
